notes.text: I'm going to begin by reading through the mission briefing.

I'm working out how to measure the wind profile: aircraft readings at its own altitude, plus drops at different heights to get the shear and veer directly, with the noisy readings best combined with impact data. Drag will come from fall time and impact, and updrafts from drops that pass through the smoke column. I'll start with a test.

I'm choosing a test release point well away from the smoke, around (300, -200) heading north, so the load lands clear of the column. I'll run drops at 30, 100 and 150 m, and maybe vary headings to tell drag apart from wind.

I'm checking the drag, since the ball only travels 106 m in 7.13 s, far less than vacuum would give, so the drag looks heavy. I'm also tracking the wind at three positions, where the direction shifts by roughly -8 degrees per 100 m, though the 4-degree noise makes that uncertain.

I'm trying a few candidate values for the wind veer and shear exponent, and the measurements are noisy enough that each estimate swings widely. My working guess is a drag coefficient around 0.03, a base wind speed of 6.2 with direction 32, and a shear of about 0.25 and veer near -15, with updraft set aside for now.

Fall times run long, so drag looks too high, and I'll try 0.027. The south-heading test has dy +6.7, meaning it landed too far north and traveled too little south, which points to excess drag or wind. The east-heading test and the north-heading test show the same pattern, with predicted displacement falling short of the measured one, so all three point toward lowering drag; I'll try 0.026 next.

I'm comparing how each test's outputs shift per 0.004 change in drag: test1 moves up 6.4 in dy and 0.27 in dt, test2 moves 6.7 in dx as drag drops, and test3 shifts dy by -5.3. Test1's dy sits at +4.2, so it needs more drag to bring dy to zero, and I'm working out what that does to dt. Test2's dx at 1.9 also needs a drag increase, and I'm figuring out by how much.

I'm working out how much drag needs to rise to close the remaining gaps in test1's and test2's dt values, landing near 0.0273. Once that's set, the leftover residuals point to the wind needing adjustment, especially the northward component and its eastward rotation.

I'm going to try a drag of about 0.0273 and rotate the wind direction clockwise to 36 degrees, then see how the residuals look.

The drag coefficient looks well determined at about 0.0273, so dt can stay as it is. The remaining problem is that every y-position runs 2 to 3 metres too far north, and the heading differs across all three tests, which points at the wind rather than anything else. The northward wind component is too large, so I'm going to rotate the wind direction clockwise from 32° to 40°, which moves more of its strength into the east.

I'm estimating how much the wind should shift the load over 7 seconds, since the load gradually picks up wind velocity and drifts. A rough guess is about 0.5 m/s of extra northward change, giving maybe 2.5 m in test 1, so I'll try the 40° direction.

I'm comparing the three tests after an 8° rotation, and test2 stands out because it was taken from 150 m, so its readings carry more weight. Once the readings are rotated to direction 32, the north offsets come out as roughly 2.4, 2.0 and 3.2. The thinking is settling on the conclusion that the north component needs to be reduced.

Working through the wind change needed to shift each test's position, I'm estimating how much the wind vector would have to change in the north-south direction for test1, test2 and test3. Test3 stands out because the low-level wind measurement points to a lower north component, though the noise in that test makes the size of the required change uncertain.

I'm checking whether the low-level wind fits a more negative veer, since the measured direction at 30 m is about 50° against roughly 32° at 100 m. Working through the fit at 100 m and 30 m, the low-level wind would need to turn further east than the hypothesis gives.

I'm checking whether a veer of about -30° would fit the low-level measurements, since the 30 m wind looks rotated further east than the 100 m and 150 m winds. I'm also considering a wind speed near 6 m/s and a shear of 0.3, while noting that I still need a few drops for updraft sampling at the operational altitudes.

I've got a first test where the vertical offset overshoots at -2.3, though the residuals look within noise. Next I need more drops to pin things down, and I'm thinking about an updraft test using a drop that passes through the smoke column, since the updraft scales with intensity and peaks at the centre.

Updraft drops come next: aim one at the origin from altitude 100 on heading 0, expecting the load to fall slower and drift differently inside the column. I'm also weighing a second drop from altitude 50 on heading 270, and I'll simulate that one with updraft set to zero first to get its offset.
The offset is (-57.3, +11.2), so the release point at (57.3, -11.2) should bring the payload to the origin if there's no updraft. I'll run both test drops to check that.

Fall time came out noticeably longer, with test4 at 8.35 against roughly 7.13 and test5 at 6.29 against 4.99, so the updraft effect looks substantial. I'll try to fit the updraft through dt and test with updraft set to 5.

I've settled the updraft at about 5.9, since both test4 and test5 hit zero near that value. Now I'm checking the positional residuals at that setting: test5 is predicted too far south by about 3 units, and its heading west at 60 m is the main thing to account for.

I'm going to fit the four wind parameters using a linear sensitivity approach, since the five drops give ten position residuals to work with. Test5's westward heading at 60 m is likely the main source of the southward error, so I'll compute a baseline and perturb each wind parameter separately to get the partial derivatives.

I'm looking at the sensitivity values: a baseline set for five targets, then a perturbed case where the first few targets shift noticeably upward.

I'm checking the sensitivity rows for the remaining targets, along with the shear and veer perturbations, and setting up the equation that combines them to cancel the baseline offsets. I'm also noting the wind measurements at 100 m, 150 m, 60 m and 30 m, and the baseline wind speed and direction model.

I'm fitting a linear trend to the measured wind directions against height, using the five points from 30 to 150 m. The slope comes out to about -0.2 degrees per metre, which is where the veer estimate is heading.

I'm working out the veer slope at about -19.6 degrees over the height range, with a standard error of roughly ±4.4. Next I'm computing the log-log speed fit against height, finding the means and the cross-product sum for the five points.

I'm working through a least-squares fit for the four unknowns (wind speed change, direction change, shear and veer), with ten equations from the targets. The measured values point to a wind speed near 5.8, direction 36, shear about 0.31 and veer around -20, and I'm going to combine those with the residuals from the drop.

I'm substituting the known ratio into the first equation, which gives the coefficient of d. The remaining equations are the rest of the system for the four unknowns, still to be solved.

I'm noting a rough noise level of about 1.5 m and a set of prior estimates for the wind and shear parameters. I'm testing a candidate with a speed change of -0.24, no direction change, shear 0.05 and veer 0.5, and checking the first few target residuals against it.

I'm checking the residuals for the last few targets against the candidate values, and the fit is still poor: the y-components for the first two targets miss by a wide margin. The drop data seem to want the speed change near zero or positive rather than the negative value I tried.

I'm setting up the normal equations for the four unknowns, laying out the columns of the sensitivity matrix and the target vector.

Computing the pairwise products for the normal equations, summing the diagonal and off-diagonal entries of the sensitivity matrix.

Still computing the normal-equation entries for the four unknowns...

Still computing the normal-equation entries for the four unknowns...

I'm setting up the prior weights for the fit: a mean of -0.24 for the speed change with a fairly tight spread, a direction prior near 0.02, and a shear prior around 0.05 with its spread tied to the speed noise.

Still setting up the normal equations, with the prior weights added to the diagonal.

I'm setting up the four-by-four system with the prior terms folded in, and starting a Gauss-Seidel pass from zero, beginning with the first unknown.

I'm running Gauss-Seidel iterations on the four-by-four system, now on the second pass, and updating the direction term from the new speed estimate.

I'm running the Gauss-Seidel iteration again on the four-by-four system, updating the first unknown, the speed change, from the latest values of the other three.

I'm running the Gauss-Seidel iteration again on the four-by-four system, updating the direction term from the new speed estimate.

I'm iterating on the system again, and the solution is settling: the speed change is near -0.04, the direction change near -0.06, the shear near -0.05, and the veer near 0.44. That puts the wind speed around 5.96, the direction around 35.4, the shear at about 0.29, and the veer at about -21.1. Next I'm checking the predicted residuals against the first target.

I'm checking the first residuals against the updated values: the x-component for the first target comes out to about -1.05, so its residual moves to roughly -0.35. The y-component for that target shifts to around -1.32, and I'm moving on to the second target's x-component.

I'm checking the residuals for the next targets against the updated solution, starting with the y-c

I'm working out the release offsets for the three drops, reversing each drop's displacement so the payload lands on target. For the 150 m, 80 m/s southward throw, the forward travel is only about 42.8 m south, which seems small given the 28 m eastward wind, so I'm checking how much the wind drift accounts for that.

I'm noting that the updraft will push the drops off course, but each one should still reach the smoke, so I'll release all three.
I'm looking at the large updraft effects here: fall times of 12.9 versus 9.85, and 11.29 versus 8.17. Next I'll set these against the H1 case with updraft, which comes in at 5.9.

I'm comparing the residuals from test 8 and test 6: test 8 has a time residual of -0.19 at a lower horizontal speed of 50 and a heading of 225, so the updraft or drag might be off for that case.

Comparing the predicted and observed landing points for test 8 against the updraft, I'm wondering whether the drag or the path through the column is what's off, since both runs still land inside it. Next I'll recompute how each test responds to drag, updraft, and the four winds so I can fit all six parameters together.

I'm setting up the linear system now, starting from the residuals for each test as (dx, dy, dt) and listing them through T7, where the last entry is still coming.

Next I'm filling in the sensitivity values for each test across the drag, updraft, WS and direction perturbations, which is mostly the same numeric table continuing.

Still filling in the sensitivity table...

Now I'm checking the drag sensitivity on T1: dy went from -1.3 to -3.0 when drag went up, and the earlier pair of runs agrees, so the direction is consistent. Next I'll weight the dt equations heavily, since their noise is much smaller than the position noise.

Now I'm writing out the dt equations with the drag and updraft unknowns, which for T1 through T3 reduce to near-zero drag terms. For T4 through T7 I'm working through each residual against the updraft, shear and veer coefficients.

Now I'm checking T8 against T6: their drag and updraft sensitivities are nearly the same, yet the dt residuals differ by about 0.21 s, roughly four times the noise. The likely cause is that T8's path changes with the wind and direction perturbations, shifting its timing.

Checking T8 against T6 again: the drag and updraft sensitivities are nearly identical, but their dt residuals differ by about 0.21 s, so a joint fit has to explain that gap through the wind and direction terms. Those terms only move T8's timing by around 0.03 s each, so they can't close the gap alone.

Checking whether T8's longer flight time could just be noise or a path effect: the drag and updraft sensitivities for T6 and T8 are nearly the same, so those terms alone can't explain the gap. I'm weighing whether a sub-0.2 s discrepancy is plausible as observation noise, or whether the radial updraft profile is responsible for T8's landing position.

Checking whether T8's longer flight could come from its path sitting closer to the updraft axis than predicted. The ground point is about 4.8 m off, so the trajectory inside the column may be different too, and a modest change in updraft exposure could plausibly account for most of the 0.19 s gap.

Now I'm working through why T8 would run longer than predicted, which the drag and wind terms don't account for. My guess is the trajectory passes closer to the updraft axis than modeled, so it spends more time in the column, and the release point at r=31 sets how much of the path falls inside it.

Now I'm estimating the drag and updraft coefficients from the dt equations alone, since T1 through T3 pin the drag term to roughly zero.

Now I'm assembling the normal equations from the dt and position residuals, summing the squared sensitivities and cross-terms for the drag and updraft unknowns.

Now I'm solving the two-unknown system for drag and updraft from the dt equations, which gives a drag of about 0.027 and an updraft of about 6.05. Even with those values, T8 and T6 still leave residuals of roughly 0.12 s and -0.085 s, both around two sigma.

Now I'm folding in the small drag and updraft corrections and checking how the remaining position offsets shift for T1 through T5.

Now I'm setting the wind coefficients a, b, c, d against the target residuals for each test, starting with T1 through T8.

Now I'm writing out the wind columns for the least-squares fit, listing each test's sensitivity to the ws and dir perturbations.

Now I'm working out the normal-equation sums, starting with the squared terms for the wind columns.

Now I'm computing the dot products for the wind columns, multiplying each test's sensitivities pairwise to fill in the normal-equation matrix.

Still working through the normal-equation sums for the wind columns, checking the cross-products as I go.

Now I'm computing the cross-product sums between the ws and shear columns, multiplying the sensitivities test by test.

Now I'm finishing the AᵀD sums for the veer column, multiplying each test's sensitivities pairwise as before.

Now I'm finishing the AᵀD sums for the veer column, working through the re

I'm seeing residuals around 1.5 to 2 meters, with the priors pulling the wind speed down and producing a dy of -2 for T1 and T2. I'm wondering whether the prior weight is simply too strong, and whether the wind measurement itself might be biased, though that isn't mentioned anywhere. T8 still has a persistent dx of 3.5 at heading 225 and speed 50, which seems poorly modeled.

I'm checking whether T8's positive dx comes from the updraft or drag, since lowering either one would fix dx but push dt the wrong way. I'm also considering whether the column radius or intensity could be the cause, though the calibration fire values look fine, and whether T8's offset is just noise at about 2.3σ.

I'm considering whether the updraft parameter might be the problem, especially with low-speed drops, so I'll fly two more test drops: one at slow speed and low altitude into the smoke, and another faster and higher from a different heading, to get variety across the flight envelope. I'll aim them using the current hypothesis with the updraft included, so they land near the center.

I'm nudging the release point by (-14.8, -31.9) to land at (25.2, -71.9), which slightly shifts the path within the column but should be close enough. Then there's a second adjustment of (-71, 46.5) to account for.

I had planned two of these, but I ended up using both. That's fine, so now I'll compare against H2 and redo the sensitivity runs around it, six comparisons plus the base, so that tests 9 and 10 get all their rows.

I'm setting up a full least-squares fit with six unknowns, covering drag, updraft, wind speed, direction, shear, and veer. The system will combine 20 position rows weighted at sigma 1.5, 10 time-step rows, and 4 priors, and I'm starting from a base residual at the first few points.

Now I'm working through the sensitivity values for each tool across the parameters, filling in the matrix row by row.

Now I'm filling in the sensitivity entries for the B parameter, working through each tool's values.

Still filling in the sensitivity matrix for the C and D parameters across the tools...

Splitting the problem into two stages: first fitting the drag and updraft parameters from the time-step rows, which only weakly depend on the wind terms, and then using those results to solve for the winds from the position rows.

I'm computing the dt-row normal-equation sums now: the p-p, p-u, and u-u entries, plus a small cross term, from the coefficient lists for the ten time-step rows.

I'm finishing the time-step fit: the cross-check gives a drag value of about -0.189 and an updraft of about 0.045, so the drag term comes out near 0.027 once scaled.

I'm weighing whether to fit drag jointly with the position rows instead of from the time-step rows alone, since the positions are also sensitive to it. The time-step estimate leaves drag fairly uncertain on its own, so I'm going to run the full six-unknown normal equations rather than keep the two-stage split.

Now I'm laying out the position-row sums for the full normal equations, pairing each unknown's sensitivities across the twenty x and y rows.

Now I'm continuing the position-row sums for the A and B unknowns, listing their sensitivities across the twenty x and y rows.

Still working through the position-row sums for the C and D unknowns, matching each row's sensitivities against the residuals.

Now I'm listing the time-step rows' coefficients for the drag, updraft, and wind terms across all ten rows.

Now I'm summing the position-row contributions for the drag unknown, squaring its sensitivities across the twenty x and y rows.

Now I'm summing the position-row contributions for the P-P entry and scaling the time-step part by 900, which brings the total to about 204.

Now I'm summing the position-row contributions for the U-U entry, starting with the T4 and T5 terms.

Now I'm summing the position-row contributions for the P-A cross term, working through the first several tools' sensitivities.

Now I'm finishing the cross-term for the P and A unknowns: the position-row total comes to about 71.6, and the time-step contribution is still being added in.

Now I'm summing the position-row contributions for the P-B cross term, which comes out to a partial total of about 8 before the remaining tools are added in.

Now I'm working through the cross-term sums for the P and B unknowns, which come to about -26.2 once the time-step part is added in. Next I'm starting the P-C position sums, beginning with the first few tools' values.

Still working through the cross-term sums for the P and C unknowns, adding the position-row totals and then the small time-step part.

Now I'm summing the position-row contributions for the P-D cross term, which comes to about -3.4 before the remaining tools are added in.

Now I'm finishing the drag sums, then moving on to the updraft entries across the position rows.

Now I'm summing the updraft-and-A cross terms over the position rows, starting with the first few tools' sensitivities.

Now I'm finishing the updraft-and-B cross term for the position rows, which starts with a small partial total before the remaining tools are added in.

Now I'm checking the updraft-and-B cross term for the remaining tools, which brings the position-row total to about -5.8 before the time-step part is added in, and then I'm starting the updraft-and-C sums.

Now I'm finishing the updraft-and-C sum: the position rows give about -23.9, and the time-step part adds roughly 0.047 more.

I'm working out the adjusted values: direction comes to 34.91, shear to 0.282, and veer to -20.16. Next I'm comparing hypothesis H3 against those numbers, with drag at 0.02686, wind speed at 5.76, direction at 34.9, shear at 0.282, veer at -20.2, and updraft at 6.16.
The mean miss of 1.85 with 1.5 noise per axis lines up with the expected Rayleigh mean of about 1.88, so the result sits at the noise floor. That checks out, and I'll move on to the operation.

I'm weighing which settings make the result least sensitive to error: a lower altitude and slower speed should both cut down on uncertainty, so I'm leaning toward the minimum of each and a mid-range heading. My plan is to simulate a release from the target, measure the offset, shift the release point by the opposite amount, and then run the simulation again to confirm, since the updraft varies with position.

I'm settling on the specific test values: heading 342, altitude 107, and speed 49, starting the release at the coordinates (466, 1076).

I'm checking whether the simulation already covers the target fires and their smoke columns after begin_operation. It reports the landing as 96 m from the fire, so I'll shift the release point by (3.4, -96.5) to (469.4, 979.5) so it starts inside the column.
I'm seeing an offset of about 1.9 horizontally and 0.2 vertically, so I'm moving the release point to (467.5, 979.3).
Hotspot 1 is aimed. Now hotspot 2.
Hotspot 2 is aimed. Now hotspot 3.
I'm off by about (5.5, 4.3), so I'll shift the release point by (-5.5, -4.3), which lands at (1158.6, -964.3). The updraft makes this nonlinear, so I'll need to iterate.
Hotspot 3 is aimed. Now hotspot 4.
Now I'm noting a horizontal shift of +0.8 on the x-axis, with the value at -1879.8.
The offset is close enough at half a metre, so I'll just apply the shift of +0.4 and +0.3, which lands at (-1023.3, 18.1). Next I'm moving on to making the drops.
All five hotspots are aimed under the fitted model. Executing drops.
